lesson.lo: use a thermometer to take accurate temperature readings and collect, record and present data as a line graph
lesson.tib: I understand how scientists measure and record changes in temperature, and how to present data clearly
lesson.isb: recording temperature data accurately in a table and plotting a line graph with a written conclusion

qna.question: What is the word for the change from gas back to liquid?
Is melting a reversible or irreversible change?
qna.answer: Reversible. Water can be cooled and refrozen back to ice.

qna.question: What do we call the change from liquid to solid?
Give an everyday example of evaporation.
qna.answer: Accept: puddles drying up, wet clothes drying on a line, sweat evaporating from skin.

qna.question: True or false — condensation is a reversible change.
qna.answer: True. Water vapour condenses into liquid, which can then evaporate again.

slides.title: Vocabulary check — what do these mean?
bullets: At what temperature does water melt from ice? At what temperature does it boil?
What is the difference between evaporating and boiling?
Can you remember the four words for the state changes? (melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing)

slides.title: How do we read a thermometer accurately?
bullets: Always hold the thermometer upright and wait for the reading to stabilise before recording.
Read at eye level — looking from above or below gives a false reading.
Record the temperature to the nearest degree and include the unit: °C.

slides.title: How will we set up the ice-melting investigation?
bullets: Place ice in a beaker. Record the starting temperature. Start your timer.
Take a temperature reading every 2 minutes. Record each reading in the table on your LP.
After 10 minutes, plot your results as a line graph — time on the x-axis, temperature on the y-axis.

slides.title: What do you think is happening here?
Carry out the investigation
bullets: Record the temperature every 2 minutes in the table on your LP.
Plot each reading on the line graph axes — join the points with a smooth line.
Write a conclusion: what happened to the temperature as the ice melted?
Challenge: explain why the temperature stayed at 0°C for a time before rising.

slides.title: Who do you agree with and why?

learners.name: Learner A
learners.statement: One measurement is enough. If you do the experiment carefully once, you'll get the right answer.

learners.name: Learner B
learners.statement: You should always repeat the measurement at least three times. One result might have an error in it.

learners.name: Learner C
learners.statement: It only matters to repeat if your first result looks wrong or unexpected.

Plot each temperature reading with a cross (x). Join the crosses with a smooth line.

sections.title: Temperature of ice as it warms up

sections.text: What happened to the temperature while the ice was melting? What does your graph show?
0 min: 0°C (or below — starting temperature of ice)
2 min: 0°C (ice still melting — temperature stays flat)
6 min: 2-8°C (ice fully melted, water starting to warm)
Key pattern: temperature stays near 0°C while ice melts (heat energy goes into breaking the solid structure, not raising temperature), then rises once all the ice has melted.

As the ice melted, the temperature stayed at 0°C for the first few minutes. Once all the ice had melted, the temperature began to rise steadily. This shows that the heat energy was being used to melt the ice rather than to warm the water.
